title: The Wrong Loss

scenario.situation: The delivery-time prediction model has an RMSE of 4.2 minutes — down from 6.8 last quarter — but dispatchers insist the model is useless for deciding which jobs to send drivers to first.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: The engineering team believes the dispatchers just need time to trust the model, and that pushing RMSE below 3.5 minutes will make the complaints go away.
scenario.question: Is RMSE the right thing to optimize, or is the model failing the dispatchers for a different reason?

decisions.prompt: The engineering team wants a plan to cut RMSE further. How do you frame your investigation before agreeing to that roadmap?

options.label: Profile the worst-error predictions
options.detail: Find the jobs where predicted vs actual delivery time diverges most and investigate those cases.
options.consequence: You identify a cluster of high-error edge cases and reduce them, trimming RMSE slightly. But dispatchers still complain — the model's ranking of jobs hasn't improved at all.
options.divergenceCost: Chased error reduction without questioning whether error was the right thing to chase.

options.label: Map the model's output to the actual dispatcher workflow
options.detail: Interview dispatchers and trace exactly how model predictions feed into job-prioritization decisions — then check whether RMSE captures that usage.
options.consequence: You discover dispatchers never look at the raw minute estimates — they use the model to rank jobs by urgency. RMSE measures point accuracy, not ordering quality. A completely different metric is needed.

options.label: A/B test the current model against a simple baseline
options.detail: Compare RMSE of the model against a naive heuristic (e.g., historical average by zone) to establish whether the model adds value.
options.consequence: The model beats the baseline on RMSE, confirming it's technically better — but still doesn't answer why dispatchers find it useless for prioritization.
options.divergenceCost: Validated the wrong dimension of performance and missed the workflow mismatch.

options.label: Collect more dispatcher feedback via survey
options.detail: Send a structured survey asking dispatchers to rate the model's usefulness and describe pain points.
options.consequence: Feedback is slow and qualitative. Dispatchers say 'the order feels wrong' but you lack the quantitative framing to act on it before the next sprint planning meeting.
options.divergenceCost: Chose a slow qualitative instrument when the mismatch was already measurable in the data.

decisions.prompt: You suspect the model's ranking of jobs is the real problem. Which metric do you use to evaluate whether that's true?

artifact.title: Model evaluation by metric — current model vs baseline
artifact.caption: Both point-error metrics show the model beats the baseline comfortably. Yet dispatchers still report wrong prioritization. Is the problem even visible here?

options.label: Mean Absolute Error (MAE) by job type
options.detail: Break MAE down across job categories to find where point-prediction error is largest.
options.consequence: MAE varies somewhat by job type, but even fixing the worst category won't change how jobs are ordered relative to each other. The ranking problem is invisible to any point-error metric.
options.divergenceCost: Sliced a metric that still can't capture whether jobs are ordered correctly.

options.label: Kendall's Tau (rank correlation) between predicted and actual job urgency order
options.detail: Measure how well the model's predicted delivery times rank jobs in the same order as their true urgency.
options.consequence: Kendall's Tau is 0.41 for the current model — barely better than random ordering. The baseline heuristic scores 0.39. Despite a 38% RMSE improvement, ranking quality is essentially unchanged. The metric mismatch is now quantified and undeniable.

artifact.title: Ranking quality: Kendall's Tau (predicted vs actual urgency order)
artifact.caption: A prototype retrained on a ranking loss (LambdaRank) nearly doubles Tau. The RMSE model offers almost no ranking advantage over guessing.

decisions.prompt: The ranking metric reveals that RMSE optimization has delivered near-zero improvement in job ordering. What do you tell the engineering team?

options.label: "RMSE is the wrong loss function — switch to a ranking objective immediately."
options.detail: Make the full causal and prescriptive call based on the prototype result.
options.consequence: The team retrains on a ranking loss and deploys quickly. Tau improves in offline tests, but without a prospective evaluation you can't confirm the prototype's gains hold on live traffic or that dispatcher workflow actually improves.
options.divergenceCost: Overclaimed from a prototype — skipped the validation step needed to confirm gains in production.

options.label: "RMSE optimization isn't improving what dispatchers need — ranking quality is flat. A prototype suggests a ranking loss helps, but we should run a prospective pilot before retraining the production model."
options.detail: Present the finding, name the metric gap, and recommend a controlled pilot as the path to certainty.
options.consequence: The team understands why further RMSE investment would be wasted and has a credible, low-risk path forward. You've reframed the roadmap with evidence and flagged what still needs validation — exactly what's needed before a production decision.

insight: The model's RMSE had improved by 38% yet delivered almost zero improvement in the thing dispatchers actually needed: correct job ordering. The real driver was a metric-to-decision mismatch — RMSE penalizes large point errors, but prioritization only requires knowing which job is more urgent than another, a ranking problem. Kendall's Tau made the mismatch quantifiable and undeniable. The lesson: before optimizing further, verify that your loss function is aligned to how the model's output is actually used — a better score on the wrong metric is wasted work.
